what: One shaft drives three phased pegs. Each peg lifts a free beater and releases it onto a fixed strike bar. One camshaft lifts and releases three gravity beaters. Compare shaft phase, falling motion and tempo.
try: Reset and run the three tempo stages. Watch a beater, its peg and the strike bar.
Count each channel’s drops during two shaft revolutions at one speed.
Compare the short-short-long rhythm at the three speeds.
why: Peg contact raises the beater; after release, gravity returns it. Mechanical 0°/90°/180° indexing sets the rhythm. Speed changes tempo while the phase pattern stays fixed. The app visualises impacts rather than synthesising sound.
matters: Cams coordinate repeated contact events with one drive, as in mechanical sequencers.
question: Does doubling shaft speed change the 90°/90°/180° spacing into equal spacing?
answer: No. The angular spacing is fixed by the physical pegs. At steady speed, all time intervals halve, preserving the short-short-long pattern.
further: Distinguish a turning shaft from a genuinely lifted and released beater.
The model does not predict tuned pitch, loudness, friction or real acoustic quality.
formula: event interval = phase gap / shaft angular speed
